subject: Archaeology
title: Space Archaeology: Beyond Earth
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Space Archaeology: Beyond Earth.

hook.text: The Moon has archaeological sites. Landing spots and footprints are heritage — unprotected.

buildup.text: Apollo 11's boot prints, flag, and equipment have not been touched since 1969.

discovery.text: NASA's 2020 act asks lunar visitors to avoid Apollo sites but cannot enforce it.

twist.text: Private companies plan Moon missions. Nothing stops a rover driving over the prints.

climax.text: Archaeologists want lunar heritage protected like Earth sites. Space is next.

punchline.text: We left footprints on the Moon. No law protects them.

quiz.question: What is the legal status of Apollo landing sites?
options: Fully protected under space heritage treaties
NASA asks visitors to avoid them but no binding law exists
They belong to the United States under the Outer Space Treaty

details.summary: Space archaeology studies human-made objects and sites beyond Earth — from Apollo landing sites on the Moon to decommissioned satellites in orbit. It also applies satellite remote sensing to discover archaeological sites on Earth from space using multispectral imaging and radar.
details.whyItMatters: Human activity in space is creating a new archaeological record. Meanwhile, satellite technology from space programs has revolutionized how we find and monitor archaeological sites on Earth's surface.
takeaways: Apollo landing sites are protected as heritage under US law
Satellite imagery discovers new archaeological sites from orbit
Human space activity creates an emerging archaeological record

faq.question: Are Apollo landing sites considered archaeological sites?
faq.answer: The US One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act (2020) protects Apollo landing sites. NASA has issued guidelines for maintaining distance from these sites. They represent humanity's first footprints on another world and are technically the earliest extraterrestrial archaeological sites.

faq.question: How does satellite remote sensing find archaeological sites?
faq.answer: Multispectral sensors detect vegetation stress, soil moisture differences, and surface composition changes caused by buried structures. Radar penetrates vegetation canopy and shallow soil. Sarah Parcak's work has identified thousands of potential sites across Egypt using these satellite techniques.
